chunks.text: 3 Problem setting and dataset 3.1 Weakly annotated few-shot setting The training set is a collection of slides from rock types C train C_{\mathrm{train}} . For each image we know only its slide identifier s s , its illumination mode m ∈ { PPL , XPL } m\in\{\mathrm{PPL},\mathrm{XPL}\} and, for XPL, its rotation angle θ \theta . We never use the rock type of a training slide, for model fitting or for model selection. Model selection uses a validation set of rock types C val C_{\mathrm{val}} that are disjoint from training. Evaluation is N N -way K K -shot classification on rock types C test C_{\mathrm{test}} , disjoint from both. All three metadata fields are produced by the acquisition itself: a slide is on the stage, the analyzer is in or out, the stage or the polarizers are turned. None requires petrographic judgement, so the setting applies to any slide archive that was digitized with its capture log. 3.2 Dataset We use the Nanjing University teaching thin-section photographs ( Lai et al., 2020 ) , the same collection as Wang et al. (2025a) . Counts below are from the released archives. Table 1: Nanjing University thin-section collection (counts from released archives). Rock class Rock types Slides Images Igneous 40 120 963 Metamorphic 40 120 972 Sedimentary 28 84 699 Total 108 324 2634 Each rock type has three slides. Each slide has eight photographs of one field of view, taken within about five minutes. Some slides have a ninth photograph and one has seven. Image 1 is PPL and images 2–8 are XPL of the same field (checked visually on one igneous, one metamorphic and one sedimentary slide). The XPL frames are geometrically aligned with each other, and only interference colours and extinction change; Wang et al. (2025a) describe them as a rotation series at 15 ∘ steps. Our method uses only the fact that they show the same field, not the angle values.

The optional ninth image shows a magenta background, consistent with XPL with an inserted compensator plate; its acquisition mode is not documented, so we exclude it. Preprocessing. Every image carries a burnt-in scale bar in the lower-right corner, and its value differs between slides (for example 500 μ \mu m and 200 μ \mu m), so magnification varies across slides. A model could use the bar as a slide-identity shortcut, as observed for supervised classifiers by Zheng et al. (2024) , so we mask the corner before cropping. Figure 1: Aligned XPL and PPL frames of one field for an igneous (anorthosite), a metamorphic (metadiabase) and a sedimentary (bauxite) slide, after preprocessing. Dashed box: one XPP anchor box; right columns: two 224-px shots it yields. Interference colours and extinction (XPL) are replaced by relief and absorption colour (PPL), while every grain boundary stays in place. File names encode the rock name. We replace every name with an opaque slide hash before training, so the training code sees only (slide, mode, angle). 3.3 Splits and evaluation protocols After preprocessing, 322 slides remain (one slide lacks its PPL image and one has XPL frames of unequal size). Following Wang et al. (2025a) , rock types are split 78 / 10 / 20 into train, validation and test. The primary split is a random permutation of rock types with seed 0, fixed before any experiment; all main results use it. Two further random splits (seeds 1 and 2) are reported in Section 6.5 . We report two protocols: • Image-level (as in prior work): support and query images of a class may come from the same slide, and therefore from the same field of view. • Cross-slide (ours, primary): in each test episode, a class’s support images come from one slide and its queries are all XPL images of its other slides (up to 14). This measures recognition of a rock type rather than re-identification of a field of view.

It follows the requirement that test data must not share images or samples with the data used to build the model ( Mendes Júnior et al., 2024 ) ; in the few-shot setting, the support plays the role of training data. Episodes are 5-way 1-shot and 5-shot, 2000 fixed test episodes; the 95% confidence interval over episodes is about ± \pm 0.5 points. Every trained configuration is run with three seeds, and we report mean ± \pm standard deviation over seeds. 3.2 Dataset We use the Nanjing University teaching thin-section photographs ( Lai et al., 2020 ) , the same collection as Wang et al. 5 Method: cross-polarization pairing (XPP) XPP builds each pseudo-class from one training slide and draws half of its shots from the PPL image at the same field location as an XPL anchor, so the only way to match shots is through what survives the change of illumination. It uses no clustering and no neighbour selection, so the false-positive mechanism described in Section 4 never arises. Figure 3: XPP framework, drawn with real slides from Nanjing collection (igneous, metamorphic, sedimentary). (a) Each unlabelled slide is one pseudo-class; its shots are one box cropped from aligned XPL frame and from PPL frame of same field. (b) One ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 embeds both views; conv1–layer3 are frozen and only layer4 is updated. (c) Shots are pulled to normalized mean of their slide’s support shots by a cosine softmax over 32 slides of each task. (d) At test time, an XPL image is described by mean feature of a 2 × \times 3 grid of crops and assigned to nearest prototype built from another slide. Network is standard; contribution lies in how pseudo-tasks are built. 5.1 Pseudo-classes are slides A pseudo-task samples N = 32 N=32 training slides as its N N ways, with K = 1 K=1 support and Q = 3 Q=3 query shots per way. A false negative occurs when two sampled slides show the same rock type. Section 4.1 shows that false negatives cost almost nothing, so we accept them rather than cluster slides, which would reintroduce false positives. 5.2 Paired views For slide s s , an anchor XPL image (one of the seven rotation angles) and an anchor box (a square of 0.3–0.6 of the image’s short side) are drawn once per task. Every shot of s s is then: • with probability 1/2, the anchor box in the same XPL image , or • with probability 1/2, the anchor box in the PPL image of the same field . Each shot is a random sub-crop of 60–100% of the box area, resized to 224 px, with random 90 ∘ rotations and flips and mild brightness and contrast jitter ( ± \pm 20%).

Hue and saturation are not changed, because colour carries diagnostic information (interference colours, pleochroism). The PPL and XPL frames of a field are geometrically aligned, so the same box covers the same grains. The box is kept fixed on purpose. Positives from other regions of the slide, or from other rotation angles, reduce accuracy (Section 6.3 ). Other regions share only slide-level properties such as overall tint and magnification, which teaches the model to recognize the slide rather than the rock. 5.3 Objective Shots are embedded and normalized, prototypes are the normalized mean of the support shots, and queries are classified by cosine similarity with temperature τ = 0.1 \tau=0.1 : ℒ = − log ⁡ exp ⁡ ( cos ⁡ ( f ⁡ ( x q ) , c y ) / τ ) ∑ n = 1 N exp ⁡ ( cos ⁡ ( f ⁡ ( x q ) , c n ) / τ ) , c n = ∑ k f ⁡ ( x n , k ) ‖ ∑ k f ⁡ ( x n , k ) ‖ \mathcal{L}=-\log\frac{\exp\left(\cos(f(x_{q}),c_{y})/\tau\right)}{\sum_{n=1}^{N}\exp\left(\cos(f(x_{q}),c_{n})/\tau\right)},\qquad c_{n}=\frac{\sum_{k}f(x_{n,k})}{\left\|\sum_{k}f(x_{n,k})\right\|} (1) 5.4 Encoder and training The encoder is an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50, the same backbone family as Wang et al. (2025a) , with the 2048-d pooled feature. Only the last stage (layer4) is fine-tuned, with AdamW (learning rate 1e-5, weight decay 1e-4), a cosine schedule and 1500 iterations. Every 100 iterations, the checkpoint is scored on 500 cross-slide 1-shot episodes of the 10 validation rock types, and the best is kept. Training takes about 6 minutes on one RTX 4090. Gentle adaptation is essential. Fine-tuning the last two stages at learning rate 1e-4 for 4000 iterations drives every label-free variant below the ImageNet features (Section 6.4 ). 5.5 Inference At test time a shot is one XPL image. Its feature is the mean of the normalized features of a 2 × \times 3 grid of square crops (side 0.5 of the short side, resized to 224 px), matching the training scale.

Queries are assigned to the prototype with the highest cosine similarity. 6 Experiments On the primary split, XPP is the best label-free method on every protocol and matches a supervised model trained on 78 identified rock types. All numbers are mean ± \pm standard deviation over three seeds unless stated. 6.1 Baselines All trained methods share the encoder, the fine-tuning budget of Section 5.4 , the validation-based checkpoint selection and the test episodes: • ImageNet features : no training on thin sections. • Instance training : pseudo-class = slide, every shot an augmentation of the same XPL box (XPP without the PPL shots). • Colour-jitter control : instance training plus SimCLR-style colour jitter (hue shift up to ± \pm 180 ∘ , saturation × \times 0.3–1.7, 20% grayscale). It tests whether the PPL view acts as a colour augmentation. • Neighbour pseudo-tasks : the PETD idea on thin sections. With probability rising to 0.6, a shot is taken from the slide’s nearest other slide in the current feature space. • Supervised : pseudo-class = identified rock type, using all 78 training types. 6.2 Main results (primary split) Table 3: Main results on primary split: 5-way accuracy (%), mean ± \pm sd over three seeds, 2000 test episodes. Averaged over the three splits, it reaches 88.08%, the highest of the label-free methods (instance training 85.69, colour jitter 86.24, neighbour pseudo-tasks 86.99) and on par with the supervised model (88.20). The ranking of the other methods is less stable. Instance training barely improves on ImageNet features on split 1 (+0.04), and colour jitter, which hurts instance training on the primary split, helps it on splits 1 and 2. On split 2, colour jitter is 0.30 points above XPP, and the supervised model leads by 2.15 points. With 20 test rock types, the choice of split moves even the untrained baseline by 3.8 points. Single-split results in this domain, including prior work, should therefore be read with that variation in mind. We report the primary split as the main benchmark, as is standard, and give these numbers so that the size of the effect can be judged. 6.6 Label efficiency (primary split) Table 7: Label efficiency on primary split: supervised meta-training with k k identified rock types versus XPP (%). XPP is the only encoder that brings the two illuminations of a field together (Table 8 ): same-field PPL–XPL cosine rises from 0.74 to 0.82, and a PPL image retrieves its own XPL field among all test fields twice as often as with ImageNet features. In a harder 20-way task (Table 9 ) (every test rock type at once, prototypes from the other slides), XPP reaches 85.71% against 79.29% for instance training. Removing colour at test time costs the supervised model 3.4 points, but neither label-free model (XPP − - 0.3, instance training +1.1). Robustness to colour is therefore a property of slide-level self-supervision in general, not of the polarization pair alone; what the pair adds is cross-illumination alignment. Grad-CAM maps (layer4, 14 × \times 14) of the three encoders are nearly identical, as expected when only the last stage is fine-tuned gently, and are given in the supplementary material.

Section 4 showed that useful positives must be correct and must differ from the anchor in ways the current features do not already discount. Feature neighbours fail the first condition; augmentations, other angles and other regions fail the second, or differ in the wrong way (slide-level tint and magnification). A PPL–XPL pair changes nearly all colour information while preserving every grain boundary, so the only shared signal is the petrographic structure that also distinguishes rock types across slides. Why acquisition metadata is not a label.

The pairing uses only the fact that two photographs show the same field. It never states what the rock is, which is the expensive, expert step. Any laboratory that captures PPL and XPL views of a field, which is standard practice, can apply XPP to an archive that has never been identified. Why this setting, with about 230 training slides. Identifying the training slides of a teaching collection would be cheap; the use case is a large digitized archive, a new drilling campaign or a multi-laboratory collection, where identification lags acquisition. The Nanjing collection is the public benchmark on which the gap to supervision can be measured. Only checkpoint selection uses identified samples, a validation set of 10 rock types; the training slides themselves are never identified. 8 Conclusions This paper addresses few-shot classification of rock thin sections when no training slide has been identified, and the only information available is the acquisition metadata recorded by the microscope. We analysed why generic unsupervised pseudo-tasks fit this setting poorly and proposed cross-polarization pairing (XPP), which uses the PPL and XPL views of the same field as positives. Evaluated on the Nanjing University collection under a cross-slide protocol, the work leads to the following conclusions and future directions. (1) Generic unsupervised pseudo-tasks are limited by their positives. Oracle experiments show that false positives, not false negatives, cost accuracy, and that label-free selection returns positives that are either wrong or near-duplicates of the anchor. On thin sections, only the PPL view of the same field is both correct and less similar to the anchor than another slide of the same rock type. (2) Cross-polarization pairing turns this property of polarized-light microscopy into a training signal.

Without any rock identification, XPP gains 4.4 points over ImageNet features and 2.0 points over instance training on the primary split, and matches a supervised model meta-trained on 78 identified rock types, on the primary split and on average over three random splits. (3) The gain comes from the pairing itself. Strong colour augmentation, other regions of the slide and other rotation angles do not reproduce it, and XPP is the only encoder that aligns the two illuminations of a field while staying robust to the removal of colour. (4) The evaluation protocol strongly affects reported accuracy. Under the image-level protocol of earlier work, untrained ImageNet features already reach 97% 5-shot accuracy, whereas the cross-slide protocol measures recognition of a rock type rather than of a field of view. With 20 test rock types, the choice of split alone moves accuracy by several points, so results in this domain should be reported over several splits. (5) The size of the gain over instance training varies between random splits, and the collection offers one field of view per slide. In future work, we plan to apply XPP to larger, multi-laboratory archives with several fields per slide and full rotation series, to extend it to mineral-scale recognition, and to remove the small identified validation set now used for checkpoint selection.
